_note: INSTRUCTOR: verify these PLAT code ranges against checkcif_reference/checkcif_alerts.json before the course. The ranges are indicative — PLATON alert numbering is not perfectly sequential by family. Use the 'codes' match type for specific high-priority alerts you want to handle precisely.
default: Look at the flagged value in the checkCIF output and ask whether it is chemically and physically reasonable. Consult the original paper for context.

rules.pointer: Data completeness / resolution: check the reported completeness percentage and resolution limit (sinθ/λ) in the checkCIF output. Low completeness can introduce systematic errors in refined parameters. Is any missing data in a systematic region (e.g. a detector blind zone or deliberate cutoff)?

Missed symmetry (ADDSYM): PLATON detected a possible higher-symmetry space group. Look at the ADDSYM output in checkCIF — which symmetry element is suggested and with what tolerance? Then open the structure in Mercury and compare the molecular packing in the reported setting with what a higher-symmetry model would look like. Is the apparent symmetry real, or are there systematic deviations that rule it out?

Absolute structure (Flack / Hooft): this is NOT visible as a 3D geometric feature in Mercury. Look at the Flack x parameter and its standard uncertainty in the checkCIF output. A value near 0 supports the reported absolute configuration; near 1 suggests the hand may be inverted; intermediate values may indicate racemic twinning or poor anomalous signal. Check whether the compound has a known stereocentre whose configuration can be independently verified.

R-factor / data quality: NOT investigated in Mercury. Compare the R1, wR2, and GooF values reported in checkCIF with the values in the original paper. Also check the data-to-parameter ratio and the number of restraints. A high GooF or large disparity between R1 and wR2 can indicate an unresolved modelling problem.

Hirshfeld rigid-bond test / residual electron density: these alerts are NOT investigated in Mercury. Look at the residual density peaks (largest positive and most negative) in the checkCIF output and, where available, in the structure-factor report. Note where the peaks are located — proximity to a bonded atom suggests a modelling error or missed split site; peaks near a void suggest possible missed solvent.

Displacement parameters (ADPs): open the structure in Mercury, then Display → Ellipsoids and set probability to 50%. Look for non-positive-definite atoms (shown as spheres or negative eigenvalues in checkCIF), unusually elongated (cigar-shaped) ellipsoids, or implausibly large or small Ueq values compared with chemically similar atoms in the same structure.

Molecular geometry (bond lengths and angles): measure the flagged bond or angle in Mercury (right-click on the bond or atom sequence → Measure distance / Measure angle). Compare with chemically expected values for this functional group — are the numbers reasonable for the stated atom types, or do they suggest a mis-assigned atom or a disorder that was not modelled?

Formula / atom count / hydrogen placement: check the molecular formula and atom count in the checkCIF output against the reported formula in the paper. Discrepancies in H-atom count are common when H atoms are added by riding model; discrepancies in non-H atoms are more serious and may indicate a missing or misassigned atom.
